definition: A finite transform that represents a sample record using complex coefficients for regularly spaced sinusoidal components. It preserves the record's information under a specified normalisation convention.
An efficient algorithm for calculating a discrete Fourier transform. It changes the calculation method, not the frequency information in the observed record.
One position in a discrete Fourier transform, associated with a particular sinusoidal frequency. Its coefficient is generally complex, retaining magnitude and phase.
example: An unpadded 1024-point transform at 1024 samples per second has bin labels one hertz apart.

definition: A tone whose frequency coincides with a DFT bin, completing a whole number of cycles in the unpadded observation. This condition is useful for simple coherent amplitude calibration.

A frequency representation whose values describe component amplitudes in the signal's original units. State whether values are peak or RMS, how real-frequency partners are combined and which window correction is used.

A frequency representation scaled in squared signal units, describing mean-square content under a specified convention. Squared voltage is not automatically electrical watts without a physical circuit relationship.

Mean-square signal content per unit frequency bandwidth. With voltage input and a frequency axis in hertz, its units are square volts per hertz; integrating over frequency estimates mean-square voltage.
An estimate of a record's power spectrum or power spectral density based on its Fourier transform. Window, detrending and scaling choices affect the interpretation.
Weights multiplied into a finite sample record before spectral analysis. Their shape changes spectral leakage and the trade-off between a tone's central feature and surrounding features.
A finite window that gives equal weight to every retained sample and zero weight outside the record. Taking an ordinary unweighted finite record implicitly applies this window.

A cosine-shaped taper used in spectral analysis and FIR design. Its periodic convention is useful for spectral analysis, while its symmetric convention includes both ends of a symmetric finite taper; state which array you use.

The mean of a window's weights, used to account for its attenuation of an appropriately bin-centred sinusoid. Tone correction also needs the correct one-sided scaling and assumptions about overlap between spectral components.
example: A periodic Hann with more than two samples has coherent gain one half.

definition: The spread of a tone across frequency bins caused by analysing a finite, windowed record. It can occur for a noiseless tone and does not imply multiple physical oscillators.
The central spectral feature of a windowed sinusoid. Its width affects how readily nearby tones can be distinguished.
A smaller spectral feature outside the main lobe of a windowed tone. Large side lobes can mask weaker components at other frequencies.
Underestimation when a tone between FFT bins is measured only by the largest bin magnitude. Correcting a window's coherent gain alone does not remove this effect.

Extending a sequence with zeros. Before spectral analysis this produces a denser frequency grid without adding observations; before FFT convolution sufficient padding prevents the linear tail wrapping into the beginning.
The ability to distinguish nearby frequency components. It depends on observation duration, window and signal conditions, and must be distinguished from the spacing of evaluated FFT grid points.
A sequence of Fourier transforms of windowed frames from a longer signal. It describes how frequency content changes over time, with a trade-off between frame duration and frequency discrimination.

A time-versus-frequency display of squared-magnitude or power-related short-time spectral values, often represented by colour. Its units depend on the chosen normalisation; a spectrogram is not automatically a PSD.
A short finite segment of a signal used for one local analysis. The number of acquired samples and their sample rate determine the observation duration inside the frame.
The number of input samples between consecutive analysis-frame starts. A smaller hop increases update frequency and overlap without shortening each frame's observation.
Reduction of sample rate by an integer factor. Reliable baseband decimation low-pass filters before retaining the more widely spaced samples, to suppress aliasing at the new rate.

Estimating values at new time positions from existing signal samples under a stated model, often a bandwidth limit. Integer-rate interpolation can be implemented by zero insertion followed by low-pass filtering with suitable gain.

Placing zeros between existing samples while interpreting the longer sequence at a higher sample rate. The zeros reserve time positions and create spectral images; low-pass filtering and appropriate gain are needed for interpolation.

A repeated spectral copy produced when zeros are inserted to increase sample rate. A reconstruction low-pass suppresses unwanted copies before further rate conversion can fold them into the wanted band.
Changing a signal's sample rate. Rational conversion combines an integer increase, suitable filtering and an integer decrease, with explicit amplitude, boundary and timing conventions.
An organisation of rate-conversion filtering that splits coefficient work into phases. It avoids calculating many contributions from inserted zeros or output positions that would be discarded.

Convolution with periodic, fixed-length boundaries: contributions beyond the length wrap and add into earlier positions. FFT multiplication gives this boundary model unless sufficient zero padding accommodates the full linear result.
Filtering a long input by convolving separate blocks and adding each full block response at its original position. Neighbouring tails overlap, and full finite output retains the final tail.

The operation that reconstructs a sample record from its Fourier coefficients. Its scaling must be paired with the forward transform's convention; NumPy's default inverse divides by the transform length.
Removing a fitted constant or trend before analysis. Constant detrending removes the record's mean, so it changes DC and must be recorded when interpreting levels or spectra.

A spectrum containing only non-negative frequencies, normally used for real input with redundant negative-frequency information combined according to the chosen scaling. DC and an even-length Nyquist endpoint are unpaired.
The scaling convention applied to transform coefficients. NumPy's default forward FFT is unscaled and its inverse divides by length; calibrated spectra may require additional signal-specific scaling.

The average of the squared sample values, in squared input units. Its non-negative square root is RMS; for voltage samples, mean square alone does not specify electrical watts without a physical circuit relationship.

For two finite real sequences, the property that their sample-by-sample products sum to zero. Their mean-square contributions can then be added without a cross-term, as with distinct real cosine basis components at the non-negative DFT frequencies.

Rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared. A vibration signal may record acceleration over time; amplitude, RMS and squared-density units must consistently refer to that measurement.

A frequency representation retaining both positive- and negative-frequency coefficients. For arbitrary complex input these sides can contain independent information; real input instead has conjugate symmetry.

The discrete frequencies at which a transform is evaluated. For a given sample rate, a longer FFT gives closer grid points, but zero padding alone does not add observation information or narrow spectral features.

Estimating values between adjacent samples along a straight line joining those samples. It is easy to compute but has limited high-frequency fidelity and spectral-image suppression compared with a well-designed reconstruction filter.

A quantified description of uncertainty in a measured quantity, based on a measurement model and relevant error sources. An interval must state its assumptions and intended coverage; FFT grid spacing alone is not an uncertainty interval.

The association of processed sample values with times in the original signal. Causal filter delay, centred offline filtering and boundary choices can place otherwise related results at different time positions.
